intro: A long melody floats over five-note groups in the left hand. Rachmaninoff plays this G major Prelude himself, letting its song climb into delicate high figures before the final chord.

sections.label: A · A melody above five-note groups
sections.mNote: The left hand ripples beneath a slow upper tune

sections.label: B · The tune moves below
sections.mNote: A lower melody sounds beneath quick right-hand figures

sections.label: A′ · G major and the first melody
sections.mNote: A tempo restores the opening over five-note groups

sections.label: Coda · High figures and a trill
sections.mNote: The right hand climbs, then settles on a trill

cues.title: Five notes to a beat
cues.text: The left hand rocks through five-note groups before the melody enters above it, marked dolce. Long right-hand notes stretch across the busy accompaniment. Little triplets in the tune set three against five.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition (1911), p. 22: Moderato, left-hand quintuplets and a dolce melody with triplets. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e0/IMSLP105591-PMLP02018-Rachmaninov_-_32_-_13_Preludes_(ed.Gutheil).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Victor keeps the first take
cues.text: On 3 May 1920, Rachmaninoff records the Prelude at Victor’s Church Building Laboratory in Camden, New Jersey. The company keeps take one and issues it on a twelve-inch record, Victor 74645.
cues.evidence: Discography of American Historical Recordings, matrix C-23985: take 1, 3 May 1920, Camden Church Building Laboratory; issued as Victor 74645. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/700009184/C-23985-Prelude_in_G_major_op._32_no._5

cues.title: The song moves downstairs
cues.text: In the middle passage, the melody slips into the lower part while the right hand keeps up quick, turning figures. Sharps and flats draw the music away from G major. A rising chromatic run carries the piano towards a pause.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, pp. 23–24: lower melody beneath right-hand figuration, chromatic run and fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: G major comes back
cues.text: The first melody returns at a tempo, again above the left hand’s five-note groups. Its long notes have their old ease; the small decorations begin to curl around them once more.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 24, final system, continuing on p. 25: a tempo and the return of the G major melody over quintuplets.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A trill above the ripples
cues.text: The right hand climbs into high, light figures, marked pp leggiero. A long trill hangs over the left hand’s last ripples. Under perdendo, the piano settles on its final G major chord.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 25: pp leggiero, high figuration, trill, perdendo and final G major chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The melody slips beneath the figures
transitions.from: A · A melody above five-note groups
transitions.how: The piano keeps its quick notes moving as the melody drops into the lower part. The right hand’s little figures continue above it, and chromatic notes carry the harmony away from G major. The bass now has the song.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, pp. 23–24: the melody moves beneath right-hand figuration in the chromatic middle passage.

transitions.title: The first melody rises again
transitions.to: A′ · G major and the first melody
transitions.how: A quiet dolce phrase slows towards a tempo. The right hand then recovers the first G major melody, while the left hand resumes its familiar five-note groups. The piano returns to the opening division between a long song and a rippling accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 24: dolce continuation, ritardando and a tempo return in G major.

transitions.title: The tune climbs into a trill
transitions.from: A′ · G major and the first melody
transitions.to: Coda · High figures and a trill
transitions.how: At pp leggiero, the right hand climbs above the returning tune. The left hand keeps its five-note groups beneath the high figures and the long trill. The marking perdendo carries the piano down to a quiet G major chord.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 25: pp leggiero, quintuplet accompaniment, trill, perdendo and the G major close.

fields.value: US public domain: the issued sound recording was commercially available by 1925; Internet Archive also applies Public Domain Mark 1.0 to the access file.
fields.note: Victor’s contemporary 1925 catalogue lists this Prelude on record 6261, which DAHR maps to the same C-23985 take 1 as the earlier single-faced 74645. This establishes publication no later than 1925, independently of the 1920 session date, and eligibility under the project’s pre-1926 US recording rule. The exact first-publication day remains unknown. The 1992 booklet retains an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any unidentified new creative contribution to the mastering is independently cleared worldwide.

composer.epithet: In exile he earned his living at the piano, while the bells of his Russian childhood kept sounding through the music he wrote.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen, newly graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 sat in the audience applauding. For a young composer, it was an excellent beginning.

His childhood had been less orderly. Born into a landowning family, he grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated; his sister Sofia died of diphtheria; schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the voices and bells that would stay with him. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a move to Moscow, under the formidable care of the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev.
